boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Dry Wood Creek record (September 2, 1861) in Operations to Control Missouri [June-October 1861]. The September 1 capture of the Fort Scott mules and Lane's withdrawal to Fort Lincoln are context. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field gives the Kansas cavalry about 600 and the State Guard column no figure; the live field reads US 600 and CS 6,000. Britton says the force sent out toward Dry Wood was about twelve hundred mounted men, and that Price had left Springfield with some ten thousand. Lane's September 3 report puts the column of Price and Rains at a figure read '0,000' in OCR to 10,000; his September 4 letter says all sources concur in about 6,000, and that he now held Fort Scott with about 800 cavalry.
claims.rationale: Estimates of the enemy by an interested commander, and a history's count of the Union reconnaissance that doubles the CWSAC figure. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Major General Sterling Price, Brigadier General James S. Rains and J. H. Lane as Colonel; the Official Records heading styles Lane Brigadier General commanding the Kansas Brigade. Britton says Lane ordered Colonels Johnson and Jennison out with the mounted force and that Rains held the timber; Lane credits Montgomery and Weer.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a history and an interested report; no automatic sole credit, and neither rank is adopted.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Confederate victory; NPS says the Union cavalry was forced to retire. Lane reports driving back the enemy's advanced guard and a gallant fight before falling back that night; Britton says the Federal officers withdrew to Fort Scott.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads total unknown (US 14; CS unknown); the live field reads 14 (US 14; CS 0). Lane reports about 5 killed and a number read 'G' in OCR wounded. A compiler's footnote cites a State Guard return of 4 killed and 16 wounded; Britton gives five killed and twelve wounded against four killed and sixteen wounded from the official reports.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. The live CS zero is not a measured loss.

open_questions: Price's report of the Fort Scott march, Rains's return, Prince's letters (No. 1 and No. 4) and maps remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live battle page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, vol. I (second edition, 1891) is a retrospective history by a Union soldier of the border army, based by its title page on the official reports; it is not independent of the report families. Lane's September 3 and 4, 1861 letters are one family of interested Union accounts; the compiler's footnote printed with the action's reports cites a State Guard return. Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
